questions.question: Which classical composer reportedly worked himself to death writing his own Requiem mass?
questions.fun_fact: Mozart died in 1791 while writing his Requiem, commissioned anonymously by a count who wanted to pass it off as his own. His student Süssmayr completed it after his death.

questions.question: Which composer continued composing major works after going completely deaf?
questions.fun_fact: Beethoven wrote his Ninth Symphony while profoundly deaf. At its premiere in 1824 he reportedly had to be turned around to see the audience applauding.

questions.question: Which composer was so superstitious about a 'Ninth Symphony curse' that he labeled his ninth as 'Das Lied von der Erde' instead?
questions.fun_fact: Mahler feared the 'curse of the ninth' that killed Beethoven and Schubert after their ninth symphonies. He tried to dodge it by not numbering 'Das Lied von der Erde' — then died while writing his actual Tenth.

questions.question: Which composer wrote a piece for piano that instructs the performer to sit silently at the instrument?
questions.fun_fact: John Cage's 4'33" (1952) consists of four minutes and thirty-three seconds of intentional silence. The 'music' is whatever ambient sound the audience hears in the room.

questions.question: Which Italian composer wrote concertos for an all-female orphanage orchestra in Venice?
questions.fun_fact: Vivaldi taught at the Ospedale della Pietà in Venice for decades. Many of his concertos, including parts of The Four Seasons, were composed for the orphan girls who performed behind iron grilles.

questions.question: Which composer's premiere of 'The Rite of Spring' triggered a famous riot in the audience?
questions.fun_fact: At the 1913 Paris premiere of Le Sacre du Printemps, the dissonant music and primitive choreography sparked such uproar that the orchestra reportedly could not hear itself play.

questions.question: Which composer was paid in herring for his work as a young choirboy in Lüneburg?
questions.fun_fact: Teenage Bach reportedly received barrels of pickled herring as part of his payment as a scholarship singer at the Michaelisschule in Lüneburg around 1700.

questions.question: Which composer reportedly stabbed his own foot with a heavy conducting staff and died of the wound?
questions.fun_fact: In 1687 Lully, conducting a Te Deum for the king's recovery, struck his toe with the long staff used to beat time. The wound turned gangrenous and he died months later.

questions.question: Which composer orchestrated Mussorgsky's 'Pictures at an Exhibition' into its famous version?
questions.fun_fact: Mussorgsky wrote Pictures at an Exhibition for solo piano in 1874. The orchestral version most people know was made by the French composer Maurice Ravel in 1922.

questions.question: Which record label famously rejected The Beatles in 1962 before EMI signed them?
questions.fun_fact: Decca's Dick Rowe told Brian Epstein 'guitar groups are on the way out'. EMI's Parlophone signed them instead, and the rest is history.

questions.question: Which iconic riff did Keith Richards reportedly record in his sleep on a cassette recorder?
questions.fun_fact: Richards woke up in a Florida hotel in 1965, hummed the riff into a cassette recorder, and went back to sleep. The tape contained the riff followed by 40 minutes of snoring.

questions.question: Which Nirvana song was famously inspired by a deodorant brand graffitied on Kurt Cobain's wall?
questions.fun_fact: Kathleen Hanna of Bikini Kill spray-painted 'Kurt smells like Teen Spirit' on his wall, referring to his girlfriend's deodorant. Cobain thought she meant rebellious teen spirit.

questions.question: Which Queen song was originally considered too long and weird to be a single?
questions.fun_fact: At nearly six minutes, Bohemian Rhapsody was far longer than typical 1975 radio singles. EMI executives wanted it cut, but Freddie Mercury refused — it became one of the best-selling singles ever.

questions.question: Which famous rock band's name was suggested by a comment that they would 'go down like a lead balloon'?
questions.fun_fact: The phrase came from either Keith Moon or John Entwistle of The Who. Jimmy Page liked it, dropped the 'a' in 'lead' to avoid mispronunciation, and Led Zeppelin was born.

questions.question: Which Beatles album cover features the band walking across a zebra crossing?
questions.fun_fact: The 1969 cover was shot in about ten minutes by Iain Macmillan from a stepladder. Paul McCartney is barefoot, which fueled the 'Paul is dead' conspiracy theory.

questions.question: Which song did Dolly Parton famously turn down letting Elvis Presley record because his manager demanded half the publishing rights?
questions.fun_fact: Dolly refused Colonel Tom Parker's demand for half her publishing. When Whitney Houston's 1992 cover became a massive hit, Parton's preserved rights reportedly earned her many millions.

questions.question: Which David Bowie persona was 'killed off' on stage at the Hammersmith Odeon in 1973?
questions.fun_fact: Bowie shocked his band and fans by announcing mid-show 'this is the last show we'll ever do', retiring the Ziggy Stardust character. Most of the band only learned about it onstage.

questions.question: Which Beach Boys album was famously a response to The Beatles' 'Rubber Soul'?
questions.fun_fact: Brian Wilson said Rubber Soul inspired him to make a complete album with no filler. Paul McCartney later said Pet Sounds in turn inspired Sgt. Pepper's.

questions.question: Which instrument is technically classified as a percussion instrument because its strings are struck by hammers?
questions.fun_fact: The piano's full name 'pianoforte' means 'soft-loud' because, unlike the harpsichord which plucks strings, its felt hammers strike strings with varying force.

questions.question: Which brass instrument was named after its Belgian inventor in the 1840s?
questions.fun_fact: Adolphe Sax patented the saxophone in 1846. Despite being made of brass, it's classified as a woodwind because it uses a single reed like a clarinet.

questions.question: Which orchestral string instrument is held between the knees rather than on the shoulder?
questions.fun_fact: The cello's full name is violoncello, meaning 'small large viol'. Its endpin, used to rest on the floor, only became standard in the late 19th century.

questions.question: Which keyboard instrument uses plucked strings rather than struck strings?
questions.fun_fact: Pressing a harpsichord key flicks a quill called a plectrum against a string. This is why a harpsichord cannot play louder or softer based on touch.

questions.question: Which instrument did Benjamin Franklin invent, made of spinning glass bowls?
questions.fun_fact: Franklin's 1761 glass armonica was so popular Mozart and Beethoven wrote for it. Rumors that it caused madness in players eventually led to its decline.

questions.question: Which electronic instrument is played without being touched, by moving hands near two antennas?
questions.fun_fact: Russian inventor Léon Theremin patented his instrument in 1928. One antenna controls pitch, the other controls volume — the player never makes physical contact.

questions.question: How many strings does a standard classical guitar have?
questions.fun_fact: The six-string layout became standard in the early 19th century. Earlier baroque guitars typically had five courses of paired strings.

questions.question: Which woodwind instrument is sometimes called the 'clown of the orchestra'?
questions.fun_fact: The bassoon's comedic reputation comes from pieces like Dukas's 'The Sorcerer's Apprentice'. Its tube, if unfolded, would stretch about 2.5 metres.

questions.question: Which instrument from the violin family is tuned a fifth lower than the violin?
questions.fun_fact: The viola uses the alto clef, the only common instrument to do so, because its range sits awkwardly between treble and bass clefs.

questions.question: Which percussion instrument uses pedals to change the pitch of its drumheads during performance?
questions.fun_fact: Modern pedal timpani let the player retune mid-piece with a foot pedal. Before this innovation, timpanists had to hand-tighten screws around the rim to change pitch.

questions.question: Which Police song was inspired by surveillance and stalking but is often misinterpreted as a romantic love song?
questions.fun_fact: Sting wrote 'Every Breath You Take' after his divorce. He has said he finds it disturbing that the song is so often played at weddings.

questions.question: Which Beatles song features a tape collage and a piano chord that lasts roughly 40 seconds at the end?
questions.fun_fact: The final E-major chord on Sgt. Pepper's closing track was played simultaneously on three pianos and a harmonium, with engineers cranking up the gain as it decayed.

questions.question: Which Phil Collins song was inspired by his divorce and famously kicks off with a long, slow build before a dramatic drum fill?
questions.fun_fact: The famous gated reverb drum sound was discovered accidentally in the studio while recording with Peter Gabriel. The 1981 track helped define '80s drum production.

questions.question: Which Don McLean song allegorically references 'the day the music died', referring to a 1959 plane crash?
questions.fun_fact: The crash killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens, and The Big Bopper near Clear Lake, Iowa. McLean's 1971 song spans over eight minutes and is full of cryptic references.

questions.question: Which Toto song's lyrics describe 'blessing' an entire African continent in its chorus?
questions.fun_fact: Co-writer David Paich has admitted he had never been to Africa when he wrote the song in 1981, basing the imagery on documentaries and his Catholic school upbringing.

questions.question: Which Eagles song's title was inspired by a real road in California, according to some band members?
questions.fun_fact: Don Henley has said the 1976 song is about the dark underbelly of the American Dream, not a real hotel — despite many theories pointing to specific buildings.

questions.question: Which Michael Jackson song features a spoken-word rap from horror actor Vincent Price?
questions.fun_fact: Vincent Price reportedly recorded his menacing voice-over in just two takes. Producer Quincy Jones paid him a flat fee instead of royalties — a decision Price's estate is said to have regretted.

questions.question: What standard speed in RPM does a typical long-playing vinyl album rotate at?
questions.fun_fact: Columbia introduced the 33 1/3 RPM LP in 1948. The slower speed allowed about 22 minutes per side instead of the few minutes on older 78 RPM shellac discs.

questions.question: Which classical conductor held the record for most Grammy Awards won by an individual until Beyoncé surpassed him in 2023?
questions.fun_fact: Sir Georg Solti won 31 competitive Grammys, mostly for his work with the Chicago Symphony. Beyoncé surpassed his individual total in 2023, taking the all-time record.

questions.question: Which album cover features a prism splitting white light into a rainbow?

answers.text: Pink Floyd – The Dark Side of the Moon
Led Zeppelin – Houses of the Holy
King Crimson – In the Court of the Crimson King

questions.fun_fact: The 1973 cover was designed by Storm Thorgerson of Hipgnosis. The band reportedly chose it from a handful of options in only a few minutes.

questions.question: Which album cover famously shows a baby underwater chasing a dollar bill?
questions.fun_fact: The 1991 cover was photographed in a swimming pool. Decades later, the now-adult baby Spencer Elden filed lawsuits over the image, which were ultimately dismissed.

questions.question: Which streaming service was launched in Sweden in 2008 and reshaped recorded music revenue worldwide?
questions.fun_fact: Spotify launched publicly in October 2008 with an invitation-only freemium model. It only entered the US market in 2011, three years later.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation 'A&R' stand for in the recorded music industry?
questions.fun_fact: A&R staff at a label scout new artists and match them with songs and producers. The role dates back to the early 20th century, when labels assigned material to singers.

questions.question: Which physical music format superseded vinyl as the dominant album format in the late 1980s?
questions.fun_fact: The CD was jointly developed by Philips and Sony and launched commercially in 1982. By around 1988, CDs were outselling vinyl LPs in many major markets.

questions.question: Which lossy audio format developed by Fraunhofer enabled the late-1990s digital music boom?
questions.fun_fact: MP3 (MPEG-1 Audio Layer III) was standardized in 1993 by Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft in Germany. Its small file sizes made services like Napster and iTunes possible.

questions.question: Which Andy Warhol-designed album cover features a peelable banana sticker on early pressings?
questions.fun_fact: Original 1967 copies of the album had a sticker that could be peeled off to reveal a flesh-coloured banana underneath. Intact early pressings are now collector items.

questions.question: Which composer wrote the opera 'The Magic Flute' shortly before his death in 1791?
questions.fun_fact: Die Zauberflöte premiered in September 1791, just two months before Mozart died. It's full of Masonic symbolism — both Mozart and the librettist Schikaneder were Freemasons.

questions.question: Which Pink Floyd album features the band burning a stunt man in a business suit on the cover?
questions.fun_fact: Stuntman Ronnie Rondell was actually set ablaze for the 1975 cover. The wind shifted on one take and burned off part of his moustache.

questions.question: Which guitar pickup type is generally known for its quieter, hum-cancelling design compared to single-coils?
questions.fun_fact: Gibson engineer Seth Lover patented the humbucker in the late 1950s. Pairing two coils wound in opposite directions cancels the 60 Hz hum that plagued single-coil pickups.

questions.question: Which national anthem uses a melody originally written as a British drinking song?
questions.fun_fact: The tune is 'To Anacreon in Heaven', a popular 18th-century London gentlemen's club song. Francis Scott Key wrote new lyrics in 1814 and it became the US anthem in 1931.

questions.question: Of these three Italian tempo markings, which indicates the slowest pace?
questions.fun_fact: Largo typically sits around 40–60 beats per minute. Even slower markings like 'grave' and 'larghissimo' exist but are less commonly used.

questions.question: Which 1981 Soft Cell hit was a cover of a 1964 Northern Soul track originally sung by Gloria Jones?
questions.fun_fact: Gloria Jones first recorded 'Tainted Love' in 1964 as an unsuccessful B-side. Soft Cell's synth-pop version spent 43 weeks on the US Billboard Hot 100, a record at the time.

questions.question: Which composer wrote almost all of his major works while serving as Kapellmeister to the wealthy Esterházy family for nearly 30 years?
questions.fun_fact: Haydn's isolation at the Esterházy palace meant he had to be original because, as he put it, there was no one nearby to copy. He wrote over 100 symphonies during his service.

questions.question: Which Austrian pianist lost his right arm in World War I and commissioned a series of piano concertos written for the left hand alone?
questions.fun_fact: Pianist Paul Wittgenstein lost his right arm in World War I and commissioned left-hand concertos from Ravel, Prokofiev, Strauss, and Britten. He is the brother of philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein.

questions.question: What is the longest section of a modern symphony orchestra by number of players?
questions.fun_fact: A standard symphony orchestra has around 60 string players out of roughly 100 musicians total. They typically include first and second violins, violas, cellos, and double basses.

questions.question: Which composer wrote a famous Symphony No. 45 in which the players gradually leave the stage during the final movement?
questions.fun_fact: Haydn's 'Farewell' Symphony was a hint to Prince Esterházy that the musicians wanted to go home to their families. The prince reportedly took the hint and granted leave the next day.

questions.question: Which legendary jazz saxophonist was nicknamed 'Bird'?
questions.fun_fact: The nickname is widely said to come from his love of chicken — reportedly stemming from an incident where a car he was riding in hit a chicken, which Parker insisted on cooking later.

questions.question: Which jazz trumpeter released the hugely influential 1959 album 'Kind of Blue'?
questions.fun_fact: 'Kind of Blue' was recorded in just two sessions with minimal rehearsal — the players were given only sketches of modal scales to improvise on. It remains the best-selling jazz album of all time.

questions.question: Which jazz pianist composed 'Round Midnight', one of the most recorded jazz standards ever?
questions.fun_fact: Monk reportedly began writing 'Round Midnight' as a teenager in the 1930s. His angular, dissonant playing style was initially dismissed as 'wrong notes' before being recognised as visionary.

questions.question: Which jazz singer was known as 'Lady Day' and famously recorded the harrowing protest song 'Strange Fruit'?
questions.fun_fact: Holiday's 1939 recording of 'Strange Fruit' depicted the lynching of Black Americans. Her label refused to release it, so she recorded it for a small specialty label instead.

questions.question: What does the term 'BPM' stand for in electronic and dance music production?
questions.fun_fact: Drum and bass tracks typically sit between 160 and 180 BPM, while house tracks usually hover around 120 to 130 BPM. DJs match BPMs to blend tracks smoothly.

questions.question: Which company released the Minimoog in 1970, helping make synthesizers portable and stage-friendly?
questions.fun_fact: Before the Minimoog, synthesizers were room-sized modular cabinets connected by patch cables. Bob Moog's compact, hard-wired keyboard version made the synth a viable touring instrument.

questions.question: Which Roland drum machine, originally a commercial flop, became the iconic sound of acid house in the late 1980s?
questions.fun_fact: The TR-808 was discontinued in 1983 after poor sales — its drum sounds were considered too unrealistic. Cheap second-hand units then powered hip-hop, electro, and dance music for decades.

questions.question: Which German group is widely regarded as a foundational influence on electronic music, synth-pop, and techno?
questions.fun_fact: Kraftwerk's Düsseldorf studio, Kling Klang, was kept so secret that for years it had no listed phone number. Their robotic stage persona inspired generations of electronic acts.

questions.question: Which hip-hop group released the landmark 1988 album 'It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back'?
questions.fun_fact: Public Enemy's production team, the Bomb Squad, layered dozens of samples per track. Tightening copyright rulings in the early 1990s made that dense sampling style nearly impossible to clear today.

questions.question: Which rapper became the first hip-hop artist to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music, in 2018?
questions.fun_fact: Lamar won for his album 'DAMN.', breaking a streak of jazz and classical winners. The Pulitzer board called it 'a virtuosic song collection unified by its vernacular authenticity'.

questions.question: Which New York City borough is most commonly credited as the birthplace of hip-hop in the 1970s?
questions.fun_fact: A 1973 back-to-school party hosted by DJ Kool Herc at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx is widely cited as the genesis moment, when he isolated and looped drum breaks for dancers.

questions.question: Which Scottish bagpipe variety is traditionally used in military and ceremonial settings?
questions.fun_fact: The Great Highland bagpipe is played standing and uses mouth-blown air. Uilleann pipes, by contrast, are Irish and use a bellows pumped by the elbow — they are played sitting down.

questions.question: Which Indian string instrument did Beatles guitarist George Harrison famously study under Ravi Shankar?
questions.fun_fact: Harrison first played a sitar on 'Norwegian Wood' in 1965, helping spark Western interest in Indian classical music. The sitar has sympathetic strings that vibrate without being plucked.

questions.question: Which Australian Aboriginal wind instrument is traditionally made from a hollowed-out eucalyptus trunk?
questions.fun_fact: The hollow tube is typically created by termites eating out the centre of a living eucalyptus branch. Players use circular breathing to sustain the drone for minutes at a time.

questions.question: Which Japanese stringed instrument has three strings and a body traditionally covered with skin?
questions.fun_fact: The shamisen is plucked with a large fan-shaped plectrum called a bachi. Historically, its body was covered with cat or dog skin, though synthetic alternatives are now common.

questions.question: How many semitones are there in a standard Western octave?
questions.fun_fact: The 12-tone equal-tempered scale divides the octave into 12 equally spaced semitones. Many non-Western traditions use systems with different numbers of pitches per octave.

questions.question: By what frequency ratio does pitch change when a note moves up by exactly one octave?
questions.fun_fact: If A4 is 440 Hz, then A5 is 880 Hz and A3 is 220 Hz. This doubling pattern is why notes an octave apart sound 'the same' in pitch class to the human ear.

questions.question: Which musical interval, made of two notes a tritone apart, was historically nicknamed 'the devil in music'?
questions.fun_fact: Medieval theorists called the tritone 'diabolus in musica' because of its harsh, unstable sound. Modern composers from Wagner to Black Sabbath have exploited that tension deliberately.

questions.question: What is the standard tuning frequency for the note A above middle C in most modern orchestras?
questions.fun_fact: 440 Hz was adopted as an international standard by ISO in 1955. Many baroque ensembles still tune to around 415 Hz to match historical instruments.

questions.question: In Western music notation, how many lines does a standard staff have?
questions.fun_fact: The five-line staff stabilised in the 17th century. Earlier medieval notation often used four lines, and Gregorian chant is still typically written that way.

questions.question: Which wooden component of a violin transmits vibrations from the strings to the body?
questions.fun_fact: The violin bridge is held in place purely by string tension — no glue. Inside the violin, a small dowel called the sound post helps transfer those vibrations to the back plate.

questions.question: What material are traditional violin bow hairs made from?
questions.fun_fact: A typical bow uses about 150 to 200 strands of horsehair, usually from stallions because mare hair is weakened by urine. Players apply rosin so the hairs grip the strings.

questions.question: Italian luthier Antonio Stradivari worked primarily in which city, now famous for violin-making?
questions.fun_fact: Stradivari built around 1,100 instruments in Cremona between roughly 1666 and 1737. About 650 survive today, and individual examples have sold for over 15 million dollars.

questions.question: Which brass instrument is sounded by buzzing the lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece and changing pitch with a slide?
questions.fun_fact: The trombone is one of the few orchestral instruments to use a slide rather than valves to change pitch. Its name comes from the Italian for 'large trumpet'.

questions.question: Which large pipe-organ component pushes air through the pipes to produce sound?
questions.fun_fact: Before electric blowers, pipe organs needed humans or animals to pump bellows. Bach reportedly had assistants pumping the air supply while he played his Leipzig church organs.

questions.question: Which 1985 charity concert was broadcast live from venues in London and Philadelphia to raise money for Ethiopian famine relief?
questions.fun_fact: Live Aid was watched by an estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide. Queen's 20-minute Wembley set is widely regarded as one of the greatest live performances in rock history.

questions.question: Which 1969 music festival was held on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York, and drew an audience of around 400,000?
questions.fun_fact: Despite the name, Woodstock was held on Max Yasgur's farm about 60 miles from the town of Woodstock itself. The original venue in Wallkill backed out weeks before the festival.

questions.question: Which annual desert festival in Nevada is famous for art installations and a culminating effigy burn, and incorporates significant electronic music camps?
questions.fun_fact: Burning Man takes place in the Black Rock Desert and temporarily becomes one of Nevada's largest cities. Sound camps blasting techno and house throughout the night are a fixture of the event.

questions.question: Which British band's 1972 'Ziggy Stardust' tour was famously chronicled in a D. A. Pennebaker concert film?

answers.text: David Bowie and the Spiders from Mars

questions.fun_fact: The film 'Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars' captured the final concert at the Hammersmith Odeon in 1973, the same show where Bowie shocked his band by announcing the persona's retirement.

questions.question: Which Madonna album, released in 1989, sparked Pepsi to pull a commercial featuring her after religious backlash?
questions.fun_fact: Pepsi had paid Madonna 5 million dollars for the campaign but cancelled it within days of the music video's release. Madonna reportedly kept the fee anyway.

questions.question: Which Italian word, used as a musical dynamic marking, indicates 'very loud'?
questions.fun_fact: Fortissimo is written as 'ff' in scores. Tchaikovsky's '1812 Overture' famously calls for 'ffff' — four f's — at the cannon-fire climax.

questions.question: How many distinct keys are on a standard full-size modern piano?
questions.fun_fact: The 88-key range, from A0 to C8, covers more than seven octaves. Steinway settled on this layout in the late 19th century, and it has been standard ever since.

questions.question: Which Swedish pop group won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with their song 'Waterloo' and went on to global fame?
questions.fun_fact: ABBA's win in Brighton catapulted them from a Swedish act to international stars. The name is an acronym of the members' first names: Agnetha, Björn, Benny, and Anni-Frid.

questions.question: Which 1980s music technology standard let electronic instruments and computers exchange performance data over a simple cable?
questions.fun_fact: MIDI 1.0 was finalised in 1983 and remained largely unchanged for nearly four decades. It sends performance instructions, not audio — which is why MIDI files are tiny compared to recordings.

questions.question: Which Beatles album was the band's first to be recorded entirely on eight-track tape?

answers.text: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band

questions.fun_fact: Earlier Beatles albums, including Sgt. Pepper's, were made on four-track machines bounced together. Abbey Road in 1969 finally gave engineers the headroom of true eight-track recording.

questions.question: Which country pioneered the modern 'K-pop' idol industry and acts like BTS and Blackpink?
questions.fun_fact: South Korea's idol-training system can put trainees through years of singing, dancing, and language lessons before debut. K-pop exports became a significant part of the country's cultural economy.

questions.question: Which conductor led the Berlin Philharmonic for 34 years from 1955 until 1989 and recorded a vast classical catalog for Deutsche Grammophon?
questions.fun_fact: Karajan was one of the first conductors to embrace the recording studio as an instrument in itself. He insisted on close-up filming of his face and hands, often with eyes closed.

questions.question: Which famous classical-music venue in Milan has been the site of major opera premieres since 1778?
questions.fun_fact: La Scala opened on the site of a former church called Santa Maria alla Scala — hence the name. It hosted premieres of operas by Verdi, Puccini, and many others.

questions.question: Which French composer wrote the orchestral piece 'Boléro', built almost entirely on a single repeated rhythmic figure?
questions.fun_fact: Ravel called Boléro 'a piece for orchestra without music'. The single snare-drum ostinato repeats unchanged for roughly 15 minutes while the orchestration gradually thickens.

questions.question: Which folk-music collector traveled the American South in the 20th century making field recordings of blues, work songs, and prison chants?
questions.fun_fact: Lomax and his father John worked for the Library of Congress, recording artists like Lead Belly and Muddy Waters. Their archive preserved styles that might otherwise have been lost.

questions.question: Which guitar effect pedal type adds a clipped, harmonically rich sound and is associated with hard rock and metal?
questions.fun_fact: Distortion arose partly by accident in the 1950s and 60s when guitarists overdrove tube amps beyond their clean limits. Dedicated pedals later let players get the sound at any volume.

questions.question: Which 1959 American Brill Building songwriting duo wrote pop hits including 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow' and 'The Loco-Motion'?
questions.fun_fact: Gerry Goffin and Carole King married as teenagers and wrote a string of hits in New York's Brill Building scene. King later went solo and recorded the landmark 1971 album 'Tapestry'.

questions.question: Which Brazilian musical genre, developed in the late 1950s, blends samba with jazz harmony and is associated with Antônio Carlos Jobim?
questions.fun_fact: Jobim's 'The Girl from Ipanema', released in 1962, became one of the most recorded songs in history. The genre's name roughly translates as 'new trend' in Portuguese.

questions.question: Which famous violinist's recordings include the 2007 incognito experiment of busking unrecognised in a Washington DC subway station?
questions.fun_fact: The Washington Post arranged the experiment with Bell playing a 1713 Stradivarius. Over 1,000 commuters passed by in 45 minutes; only a handful stopped to listen, and he earned about 32 dollars.

questions.question: Which type of microphone is most commonly preferred in professional studios for recording vocals due to its sensitivity?
questions.fun_fact: Large-diaphragm condensers capture more high-frequency detail than dynamic mics but require external phantom power. Dynamic mics like the Shure SM58 are still preferred for live vocals because they handle loud sources without distortion.

questions.question: A guitarist plays a string, then lightly touches its exact midpoint without pressing down. What surprising thing happens to the sound?

answers.text: It jumps up one octave higher
It drops down one octave lower
It stops making any sound at all

questions.fun_fact: This trick is called a natural harmonic. Touching the midpoint mutes the fundamental and lets only the doubled-frequency overtone ring, so the note leaps an octave even though no fret is pressed. Touching at one-third of the length yields a note an octave-and-a-fifth up.

questions.question: Why does helium make your singing voice sound high and squeaky?

answers.text: Sound travels faster through it, raising the resonant pitches
It physically shrinks your vocal cords
It makes your vocal cords vibrate twice as fast

questions.fun_fact: Your vocal cords vibrate at the same frequency in helium as in air, so the fundamental pitch barely changes. What shifts are the resonances of your vocal tract: sound moves about three times faster in helium, raising those resonant frequencies and giving the cartoonish 'Donald Duck' timbre.

questions.question: Why does a tuning fork have two prongs instead of one?

answers.text: The two prongs cancel each other's recoil so it rings far longer
Two prongs are needed to produce two notes at once
The second prong doubles the volume of the note

questions.fun_fact: The prongs vibrate in opposite directions, so the sideways forces on the handle cancel out. This means almost no energy leaks away through your hand, letting a tuning fork hum its pure tone for a remarkably long time.

questions.question: What is physically happening to a wine glass when a singer shatters it with their voice?

answers.text: The voice matches the glass's resonant frequency until it flexes apart
The sound heats the glass until it cracks
Air pressure from the note crushes the glass inward

questions.fun_fact: Every wine glass has a natural resonant frequency you can hear by tapping it. If a singer holds exactly that pitch loudly enough, the glass flexes a little more with each sound wave until the vibrations exceed what it can bend, and it shatters.

questions.question: Why do orchestras tune to the oboe rather than another instrument?

answers.text: Its pitch is stable and its piercing tone cuts through the whole ensemble
It is the oldest instrument in the orchestra
It is the only instrument that cannot be retuned mid-performance

questions.fun_fact: The oboe's reed gives it a very steady pitch that doesn't drift much with temperature, and its bright, penetrating tone is easy for everyone to hear over the others. Its sustained 'A' became the practical reference note for the whole orchestra.

questions.question: When you hum with your mouth closed, where is the sound actually coming out?
questions.fun_fact: With your lips sealed, the only open path for the sound to escape is up through your nasal cavity and out your nostrils. Pinch your nose shut while humming and the sound almost completely stops, which is why you can't hum with a blocked nose.

questions.question: Why does a deeper, lower-pitched sound travel through walls and floors better than a high one?

answers.text: Its longer waves lose less energy passing through solid material
Low sounds are always played louder than high ones
Bass notes are attracted to solid objects

questions.fun_fact: Low-frequency bass has long wavelengths that are harder for a wall to absorb or block, so they pass through with less loss. High frequencies have short waves that get scattered and soaked up easily, which is why you mostly hear the thumping bass from a neighbour's party.

questions.question: What does rosin, rubbed on a violin bow, actually do to the horsehair?

answers.text: Makes it sticky so it grips and releases the string thousands of times a second
Makes the hair slippery so it glides smoothly
Tightens the hair so it stays in tune

questions.fun_fact: Bare horsehair is too slippery to make a string sing. Rosin makes the hair grab the string and drag it sideways, then let go, then grab again, hundreds or thousands of times per second. This rapid stick-slip motion is what sets the string vibrating.

questions.question: Why can't you tell which direction very deep bass sounds are coming from?

answers.text: Their long waves reach both ears almost identically
Bass sounds travel too fast for the brain to locate
Low sounds bypass the ears and enter through the body

questions.fun_fact: Your brain locates sound partly by comparing tiny timing and loudness differences between your two ears. Deep bass has wavelengths many metres long, so it bends around your head and hits both ears nearly the same way. This is why a home theatre needs only one subwoofer, but multiple smaller speakers.

questions.question: Why does your own recorded voice sound strange and unfamiliar to you?

answers.text: You normally hear it partly through your skull bones
Recordings always play back slightly faster

questions.fun_fact: When you speak, sound reaches your inner ear two ways: through the air and through the bones of your skull. Bone conduction carries extra low frequencies, making your voice sound deeper to you. A recording only captures the airborne version, so it sounds thinner and higher than you expect.

questions.question: Why does a guitar string sound higher when you press it down at a fret?

answers.text: You shorten the vibrating length, so it vibrates faster
Pressing increases the tension of the string
Your finger adds energy that raises the pitch

questions.fun_fact: Pressing a string against a fret shortens the part that's free to vibrate. A shorter length vibrates more times per second, raising the pitch. This is why frets get closer together as you move up the neck: each one shortens the string by the same proportion, not the same distance.

questions.question: Why do brass instruments like the trumpet get warmer and go sharp the longer you play them?

answers.text: Your warm breath heats the air inside, speeding up the sound
The metal expands and tightens the valves
The mouthpiece slowly loosens with use

questions.fun_fact: Sound travels faster through warmer air, which raises the pitch of every note. As you blow warm breath through a cold trumpet, the air column heats up and the instrument drifts sharp, which is why players warm up and then nudge their tuning slide out.

questions.question: What makes a mute change a trumpet's sound when it's pushed into the bell?

answers.text: It blocks and reshapes which frequencies escape
It physically slows the player's air
It cools the air to lower the pitch

questions.fun_fact: A mute partly blocks the bell and absorbs or reflects certain frequencies, letting others through. This filters the tone, taming the loud, bright high harmonics and producing the nasal, buzzy or distant sound used so famously in jazz.

questions.question: Why does blowing across the top of a bottle make a note, and why does a fuller bottle sound higher?

answers.text: The air inside resonates, and less air vibrates faster
The water itself vibrates to make the tone
Your breath echoes off the bottom of the bottle

questions.fun_fact: Blowing across the opening sets the column of air inside vibrating like a spring. A bottle with more water has a smaller air pocket, which vibrates faster and gives a higher note. Tapping the same bottle does the opposite: more water means more mass and a lower tapped pitch.

questions.question: Why do two slightly out-of-tune strings produce a wavering, pulsing sound?

answers.text: Their waves drift in and out of step, adding then cancelling
One string is physically vibrating the other
The human ear cannot hold two pitches at once

questions.fun_fact: When two pitches are very close, their sound waves slowly slip in and out of alignment. When they line up they reinforce and get louder; when opposed they cancel and get quieter. The result is a regular throb called 'beats', and tuners listen for it to slow and stop as the strings match.

questions.question: What does the curled-up tube of a French horn or trumpet actually accomplish?

answers.text: It packs a long air column into a compact, holdable shape
The curls add a spinning vibration to the tone
Each loop produces a different note

questions.fun_fact: The pitch of a brass instrument depends mainly on the total length of its tubing. A trumpet uncoiled is over a metre and a half long, and a French horn unwound stretches several metres. Coiling that length into loops keeps the instrument playable without changing the note.

questions.question: Why does a struck cymbal keep ringing long after the drum next to it has gone silent?

answers.text: Its stiff metal vibrates with very little energy loss
Cymbals are hit much harder than drums
The air around a cymbal keeps pushing it

questions.fun_fact: A drumhead is stretched skin that flexes easily and quickly hands its energy to the air, so the sound dies fast. A cymbal is rigid metal that vibrates in many overlapping modes and loses energy slowly, letting it shimmer and decay for many seconds.

questions.question: Why does a piano sound 'wrong' and tinny if every note is tuned to its exact mathematical frequency?

answers.text: Real strings are stiff, so their overtones run slightly sharp
Pianos can only be tuned by ear, never by maths
The wooden case distorts perfect frequencies

questions.fun_fact: Real piano strings are stiff, so their overtones are stretched slightly sharper than pure maths predicts. To make octaves sound right to the ear, tuners deliberately tune the high notes a touch sharp and the low notes a touch flat, a practice called 'stretch tuning'.

questions.question: What is the buzzing object that actually makes the sound in a clarinet or saxophone?

answers.text: A thin reed that flutters against the mouthpiece
A spinning metal disc inside the mouthpiece

questions.fun_fact: A single reed, usually shaved from cane, vibrates rapidly against the mouthpiece opening, chopping the airflow into pulses that set the air column ringing. The reed opens and closes hundreds of times per second, and players carry spares because reeds wear out and crack.

questions.question: Why can a soprano singing the very highest notes sometimes be heard clearly over a full, loud orchestra?

answers.text: Trained singers concentrate energy in a frequency band the orchestra is weak in
The orchestra always plays quietly under a soprano
High notes physically travel faster than low ones

questions.fun_fact: Trained operatic singers develop the 'singer's formant', a cluster of resonance around 2,800 to 3,400 hertz where the orchestra produces relatively little energy and the human ear is especially sensitive. The voice slots into that gap and carries over the ensemble without a microphone.

questions.question: Why does a drum sound completely dead and toneless out in open air with no surfaces nearby?

answers.text: No surfaces reflect the sound back, so there is no reverberation
Open air mutes low frequencies entirely
Wind pulls the sound away from the drum

questions.fun_fact: Indoors, walls, floors and ceilings bounce sound back so notes blend and linger as reverberation. In a wide open field there's nothing to reflect the sound, so it spreads out and vanishes, leaving instruments sounding flat and lifeless. Concert halls are shaped specifically to control these reflections.

questions.question: Why do headphones with active noise cancelling fight outside noise instead of just blocking it?

answers.text: They play a mirror-image wave that cancels the incoming sound
They vibrate to shake the noise apart
They speed up the sound so your ear misses it

questions.fun_fact: A tiny microphone listens to the incoming noise, and the headphone instantly plays a sound wave that is its exact opposite. Where one wave pushes, the other pulls, and the two add up to near-silence. It works best on steady low drones like an aeroplane engine and struggles with sudden, unpredictable sounds.

questions.question: Why does a string player's vibrato make a note sound richer rather than just wobbly?

answers.text: The pitch wavers around a centre the ear settles on
It physically adds more strings to the vibration
It makes the note louder with each wobble

questions.fun_fact: Vibrato rocks the pitch slightly up and down by rolling the finger on the string. The ear averages this into a single, warmer-sounding note, and the constant tiny changes help the sound carry and stand out against an orchestra, much as a flickering light catches the eye more than a steady one.

questions.question: Why does a double bass need such a huge body compared to a violin?

answers.text: Big, slow sound waves need a large surface to move enough air
The body must be heavy to hold the thick strings' tension
A larger body is purely for the player to lean on

questions.fun_fact: Low notes are long, slow waves, and pushing that much air efficiently takes a large vibrating surface. A violin's small body would barely move the air at bass frequencies, so the instrument grows huge to project its deep notes, and even then much of the lowest energy is felt as much as heard.

questions.question: Why does plucking a string near the bridge give a thinner, brighter, more nasal tone?

answers.text: It favours the higher overtones over the deep fundamental
The string is tighter near the bridge
The bridge adds a metallic ring to every note

questions.fun_fact: Where you pluck a string decides which overtones it favours. Pluck near the middle and the deep fundamental dominates, giving a round, mellow tone. Pluck close to the bridge and you excite the higher harmonics, producing the bright, biting, nasal sound guitarists and harpsichords use for contrast.

questions.question: The word 'jazz' originally had nothing to do with music. What did it first mean in early-1900s slang?
questions.fun_fact: The earliest printed uses of 'jazz' appear around 1912 in baseball writing, meaning vigour or spirit, before the term attached itself to the new music coming out of New Orleans.

questions.question: The disc jockey term 'DJ' aside, where does the word 'turntable' literally come from?

answers.text: A railway term for switching engines

questions.fun_fact: The name is pure description: a flat surface that rotates. Railways did use 'turntables' to spin locomotives around, and the audio device borrowed the everyday word for the same reason.

questions.question: The 'Mellotron', a keyboard heard on many 1960s records, made sound in a surprising way. How did it work?

answers.text: Each key played a strip of pre-recorded tape
It used tiny tuned tuning forks
It blew air across glass tubes

questions.fun_fact: Pressing a Mellotron key dragged a length of magnetic tape across a playback head, replaying a real recording of a flute or violin. Hold too long and you ran out of tape, so notes had a strict time limit.

questions.question: The Fender 'Stratocaster' guitar was partly shaped the way it is for a very practical reason. What was it?

answers.text: Its contours were carved so it wouldn't dig into the player's ribs
It was shaped to float if dropped in water
Its curves were copied from a violin for tradition

questions.fun_fact: Earlier slab-bodied guitars pressed uncomfortably against the player. Leo Fender's team added the body contours after performers complained, making comfort, not looks, the original driver of the iconic shape.

questions.question: The word 'piano' is short for 'pianoforte'. What do those two Italian roots literally describe?
questions.fun_fact: The instrument was a breakthrough because, unlike the harpsichord, it could play both quietly ('piano') and loudly ('forte') depending on touch. Its full original name advertised that single revolutionary feature.

questions.question: The 'gramophone' record got its spiral groove for a reason most people never think about. Why a spiral?

answers.text: So a single continuous track could spiral inward without lifting the needle
Because spirals were cheaper to stamp than circles
To match the spiral shape of the human ear

questions.fun_fact: A single spiral lets the needle travel steadily from edge to centre across one unbroken path. Concentric rings would force the needle to jump between separate circles, which no playback arm could do smoothly.

questions.question: Before the metronome, what objective tool did musicians lack that Maelzel's 1815 device finally gave them?

answers.text: A repeatable, steady beat to practise against
A way to navigate ships by sound at sea
A heartbeat monitor for use by doctors

questions.fun_fact: Early pendulum tempo devices existed before Maelzel's famous 1815 patented design. The goal was always the same: give musicians an objective, repeatable beat instead of relying on a teacher's swinging hand or foot.

questions.question: The 'ukulele' got its Hawaiian name, often translated as 'jumping flea', for a surprising reason. What inspired it?

answers.text: The rapid jumping movement of the player's fingers
The insects that lived in early island instruments
A dance where performers hopped on one foot

questions.fun_fact: The instrument arrived with Portuguese immigrants in the 1880s. Hawaiians reportedly named it for how a skilled player's fingers darted across the strings like a flea, a vivid description rather than a literal pest problem.

questions.question: The 'A side' and 'B side' of a single exist because of a basic physical fact about early records. What was it?

answers.text: A disc has two playable faces
Records were graded A or B by sound quality
The letters marked which way to load the player

questions.fun_fact: With two sides to fill, labels put the song they were promoting on the 'A side' and a lesser track on the 'B side'. Some B sides accidentally became bigger hits than the songs they were meant to support.

questions.question: The word 'orchestra' originally referred not to a group of musicians but to what?

answers.text: A semicircular space in front of an ancient Greek stage
A type of large stringed instrument

questions.fun_fact: In ancient Greek theatres, the 'orchestra' was the ground-level area where the chorus danced and sang. Only much later did the word shift to mean the body of instrumentalists who eventually occupied that same front space.

questions.question: The electric guitar was invented largely to solve one practical problem. What was it?

answers.text: Acoustic guitars were too quiet to be heard over big bands
Acoustic guitars went out of tune in hot venues
Acoustic guitars were too expensive to mass-produce

questions.fun_fact: In 1930s dance bands, guitarists were drowned out by horns and drums. Amplifying the strings with a pickup let the guitar finally cut through, which is why early electric models prized volume over tone.

questions.question: The 'wah-wah' guitar pedal got its name in the most literal way possible. How?

answers.text: It was named after its inventor, Walter Wah

questions.fun_fact: The pedal sweeps a tone filter as you rock your foot, producing a vocal-like 'wah' sound. The effect was reportedly discovered while engineers were trying to imitate a muted trumpet.

questions.question: The 'concert pitch' standard exists partly because, before it, the same written note sounded different where?

answers.text: On stringed versus wind instruments only

questions.fun_fact: Before international agreement, an 'A' in one town could be noticeably higher or lower than the same note elsewhere, so a singer travelling between cities might find a piece suddenly too high to sing. Standardising pitch fixed that chaos.

questions.question: The 'banjo' descends most directly from instruments brought to the Americas by whom?
questions.fun_fact: The banjo's gourd-bodied, skin-headed ancestors came from West Africa with enslaved people. Only later did the instrument become a fixture of American folk and minstrel music, far from its true origins.

questions.question: The 'tin whistle' or 'penny whistle' earned its 'penny' name for what reason?

answers.text: Early mass-produced ones cost about a penny
Players left them out to collect pennies
They were made from melted-down coins

questions.fun_fact: In 19th-century Britain, cheap tinplate whistles sold for roughly a penny, making music accessible to almost anyone. The throwaway price, not the material's value, gave the instrument its enduring nickname.

questions.question: The 'concertina' and accordion both make sound using the same hidden mechanism. What is it?
questions.fun_fact: Squeezing the bellows pushes air past free metal reeds that vibrate to make pitch, the same principle as a harmonica. The keys or buttons simply choose which reeds the air is allowed to reach.

questions.question: The word 'album', for a collection of songs, came from an older meaning. What did an 'album' first hold?

answers.text: A bound book of blank pages or pockets
A list of approved court musicians
A type of white ceremonial robe

questions.fun_fact: Early 78 RPM records held only minutes per side, so multiple discs were sold together in bound book-like 'albums' of sleeves. When the long-playing record arrived, the name stuck even though the book was gone.

questions.question: The 'kazoo' changes your voice into a buzz using what hidden part?

answers.text: A coiled spring inside the tube

questions.fun_fact: You don't blow a kazoo, you hum into it. Your voice rattles a thin membrane, adding the buzzy timbre. Stop humming and blow, and nothing happens, which is why so many first-time players are baffled.

questions.question: The 'sustain pedal' on a piano produces its effect by doing what to the strings?

answers.text: Lifting the dampers off so strings keep ringing
Pressing extra felt onto the strings

questions.fun_fact: Normally a felt damper falls onto each string when you release a key. The right pedal raises all dampers at once, so notes ring on and even strings you didn't play vibrate in sympathy, enriching the sound.

questions.question: The 'recorder', the simple school flute, got its English name from an old meaning of 'record'. What did that word mean?

answers.text: To sing or warble, as a bird does

questions.fun_fact: In late medieval English, 'to record' could mean to practise a tune quietly or to sing like a bird. The instrument took its name from that sense long before 'record' came to mean storing sound.

questions.question: The standard symphony orchestra tunes to the oboe at the start of a concert for a practical reason. Why the oboe?

answers.text: Its pitch is stable and its tone cuts clearly through
It is always the most expensive instrument present
It is the only instrument that cannot retune itself

questions.fun_fact: The oboe holds its pitch reliably and its penetrating, reedy tone is easy for everyone to hear over a noisy stage. By tradition it sounds the tuning 'A', and the rest of the orchestra matches it.

questions.question: The 'whammy bar' or tremolo arm on an electric guitar was originally added to imitate what?

answers.text: The vibrato of a singer or violinist
The wail of a police siren

questions.fun_fact: The bar slackens and tightens the strings to wobble the pitch, mimicking the expressive vibrato of the human voice or a bowed string. The confusingly named 'tremolo arm' actually produces vibrato, not tremolo.

questions.question: The 'a cappella' style of singing without instruments has a name that literally points to where it came from. What does 'a cappella' mean?

answers.text: In the manner of the chapel

questions.fun_fact: The Italian phrase means 'in the chapel style', recalling church music sung by voices alone. The term survives today for everything from doo-wop to choirs, long detached from its religious roots.

questions.question: The guitar 'slide' (bottleneck) technique in blues traces partly to a homemade instrument played how?

answers.text: A single wire nailed to a wall or board, plucked and slid
A clay pot struck with wooden spoons
A stretched animal bladder blown like a horn

questions.fun_fact: The 'diddley bow', a single string tensioned on a porch wall or plank, was a common first instrument in the rural American South. Sliding a bottle or bone along the wire produced the swooping pitches that fed into bottleneck blues guitar.

questions.question: The Beatles' song 'Yesterday' is one of the most-covered songs in history. Roughly how many recorded cover versions does it have?
questions.fun_fact: Guinness World Records has long cited 'Yesterday' as having well over 2,000 recorded cover versions. Paul McCartney dreamed the melody and worried he had subconsciously stolen it from someone else.

questions.question: Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' is the best-selling album ever. It is estimated to have sold over how many copies worldwide?
questions.fun_fact: 'Thriller' is estimated to have sold around 70 million copies. At its 1980s peak it was reportedly selling about a million copies a week.

questions.question: Which composer is shown in this 1820 painting?
questions.fun_fact: Beethoven sat for Joseph Stieler only a few times and worked on the Missa solemnis between sittings — the manuscript in his hand carries exactly that title.

questions.question: Which Italian city did the maker of this violin work in?
questions.fun_fact: Antonio Stradivari built around 1,100 instruments in Cremona, of which some 650 survive. Why they sound the way they do is still unsettled — varnish, wood density and the cold summers of those decades have all been offered as the explanation.

questions.question: Which device did this man present in 1877?
questions.fun_fact: Edison's phonograph recorded onto a cylinder wrapped in tinfoil. The first recording in history was his own recital of “Mary Had a Little Lamb” — and playing it back once already half destroyed it.

questions.question: What is on this sheet?
questions.fun_fact: Beethoven's musical handwriting was notorious: crossed out, pasted over, pressed so hard the pen went through the paper. Copyists at times refused to work from his manuscripts.

questions.question: Which keyboard instrument is shown here?
questions.fun_fact: A harpsichord plucks its strings rather than striking them, so it stays at one volume however hard you press. That is exactly what made the piano attractive from about 1700: it could finally play loud and soft.

questions.question: How many keys does a modern piano have?
questions.fun_fact: 52 white and 36 black. More would be possible, but past 88 the ear hears the lowest notes as rumble rather than pitch.

questions.question: How many strings does a concert harp have?
questions.fun_fact: 47 strings and seven pedals, each retuning one note across every octave. A harpist effectively plays the key signature with their feet.

questions.question: How many symphonies did Joseph Haydn write?
questions.fun_fact: 104 confirmed. Mozart managed 41 and Beethoven 9 — the count fell as the individual symphony grew longer and weightier.

questions.question: How many seconds does John Cage's piece last in which not a single note is played?
questions.fun_fact: Four minutes and 33 seconds of silence. The piece is notated, copyrighted, and has been litigated over more than once.

questions.question: Roughly how many minutes does Beethoven's 9th Symphony run?
questions.fun_fact: About 70 minutes. Legend says that is exactly why a CD holds what it holds — never proven, never quite denied either.
